title: Painting air-dry clay with coloured slips
subtitle: How to mix and apply clay slips tinted with pigment for earthy, integrated surface colour
excerpt: Coloured slips are diluted clay mixed with pigment. Applied to a leather-hard piece, they dry to a matte, earthy finish that sits in the clay surface rather than sitting on top of it. The finish is more durable than acrylic paint on raw clay because the slip bonds with the clay body.
sourceNotes: Coloured slip painting for air-dry clay derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: Clay diluted with water to a brushable consistency; the base for coloured slip painting
The ideal stage for slip application: the clay accepts the slip without distorting
Fully dried clay, ready for sealing or final finishing

content.text: A coloured
slip

is the same clay as the piece you are decorating, diluted with water and tinted with pigment. Because it is the same material as the clay body, it shrinks at the same rate during drying and bonds to the surface as the two dry together. Slip painting produces a matt, mineral finish. It does not look like paint; it looks like a natural part of the clay.
Mixing coloured slip

Break off a 50 g piece of air-dry clay and mix it with water until you have a pourable but not watery consistency, roughly double cream. Stir in pigment to the target colour. Powdered acrylic pigments and iron oxides both work. Start with 5-10% pigment by weight and adjust to taste. Make more slip than you think you need; running out mid-coat leaves visible brush seams.
What you need
A leather-hard air-dry clay piece
Coloured slip: air-dry clay thinned with water and mixed with powdered pigment
A broad mop brush for covering large areas evenly
A liner brush for fine detail or contrast lines
PVA varnish for sealing after the slip is bone-dry
Step-by-step
Make sure the piece is at
leather-hard
stage: firm but not bone-dry. Slip applied to a bone-dry surface does not bond as well; applied to a too-soft surface, it may distort the piece.
Apply the first coat of coloured slip with a mop brush in long, even strokes. Cover the whole surface in one direction. The coat should be thin enough to see the base clay colour through it.

Allow to dry until the slip surface looks a consistent matte colour and is no longer shiny. Apply a second coat in the opposite direction. Two thin coats gives better colour depth and coverage than one thick coat, which can crack as it dries.
For contrast designs, use a liner brush loaded with a second colour to paint lines or motifs over the first dried layer. Slip over slip bonds well at leather-hard stage.
Allow the piece to reach bone-dry fully before sealing. Sealing a still-damp slip layer traps moisture under the varnish and causes bubbling or flaking.

Seal with PVA varnish diluted 50/50 with water for the first coat. Apply undiluted PVA for the second coat. The diluted first coat soaks into the slip surface; the undiluted second coat forms the protective layer.
What the finish looks like when it is right
Dried slip is matte, even in colour, and slightly lighter in tone than when wet. At
bone-dry
the surface should show no darker patches, no brush seams, and no cracking. After sealing, the colour deepens slightly and the surface becomes smooth and water-resistant.
Common mistakes
Slip too thick. Thick slip cracks into fine crazing as it dries, particularly on curved surfaces. If the slip does not flow evenly off the brush tip, add more water.

Working on too-dry clay. On a piece approaching bone-dry, the slip dries at the brush before it can bond, leaving a powdery layer that rubs off. Dampen the surface slightly with a sponge before applying slip to very dry clay.
Using acrylic paint instead of slip. Acrylic sits on top of the clay surface and peels at the clay-paint boundary as the clay continues to dry and shrink. Slip bonds as part of the clay body.
